name: Optional values
summary: A type that says a value may be missing, so the compiler makes you handle “nothing” before you use it, instead of a null that crashes at run time.
howItWorks: In many older languages every reference can secretly be `null`, and using one throws (`NullPointerException` in Java, `NullReferenceException` in .NET). Optional values move “might be missing” into the type, where the compiler can see it. There are two ways to do it. A wrapper type is a separate value you must open: `Option<T>` in Rust (`Some(x)` or `None`), `Maybe a` in Haskell (`Just x` or `Nothing`), `Optional<T>` in Java. Rust has no null references at all; an optional pointer is `Option<Box<T>>`, and for such types Rust guarantees the wrapper has the same size as the plain pointer. The other way marks the type with `?`: `String?` in Kotlin and C#, `Int?` in Swift, `T | undefined` in TypeScript with `strictNullChecks`. The plain type then means “never null”, and the compiler only lets you use a `?` value after a check, a safe call (`?.`) or a fallback (`?:` in Kotlin, `??` in Swift and C#). Kotlin and TypeScript report errors; C# reports warnings, and its nullable reference types are entirely a compile-time feature, so the program runs the same. Every language keeps an escape hatch for when you know better (`!!` in Kotlin, `!` in C#, Swift and TypeScript, `unwrap` in Rust, `fromJust` in Haskell), and each one brings back the crash if you are wrong.
analogy: A pickup slip from a parcel locker that says either “parcel inside” or “empty”. You read the slip before walking over. A null is a slip that always says “parcel inside”, even when the locker is empty, so you only find out when you open the door.
useWhen: A lookup or parse that can legitimately find nothing: a user by id, a config key, `find` on a list
Return types of public methods, so callers can’t forget the empty case
New code in Kotlin, Swift, C# or TypeScript: turn the checker on (`<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`, `strictNullChecks`) from the first commit
avoidWhen: Java fields and method parameters: `Optional` was designed as a return type; use overloads or a nullable field
A failure that needs a reason: `None` can’t say what went wrong, so return a `Result` or `Either`, or throw
Silencing the checker with `!`, `!!` or `unwrap` everywhere, which brings the run-time crash back
example: A TypeScript app looks up the logged-in user with `users.find(u => u.name === loggedInUsername)` and then reads `loggedInUser.age`. With `strictNullChecks` off, `find` is typed as always returning a user, the code compiles, and it fails at run time when nobody matches. With it on, `find` returns `User | undefined`, and the compiler stops the build with error 18048, `'loggedInUser' is possibly 'undefined'`. Adding `if (loggedInUser !== undefined)` before the read fixes it: inside that type guard, the type narrows to the user type.

sections.title: “Maybe missing” in seven languages
sections.intro: The same idea, written as a wrapper (Java, Rust, Haskell) or as a mark on the type (Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Swift).

rows.label: Java
values: Nothing: an `Optional` variable can itself be `null`, so the rule is that it never should be

sections.title: Nullable reference types in C#
sections.intro: With `#nullable enable`, `string?` and `string` are different promises. The commented line compiles, but with warning CS8602 (“Dereference of a possibly null reference”). Run it with `dotnet run optional.cs` on .NET 10.
source: // string? says: this method may return null
emails.TryGetValue(user, out var email) ? email : null;
// Console.WriteLine(bob.Length);           // warning: bob may be null here
Console.WriteLine(ada.Length);          // 15: no warning, the check proved it non-null

sections.title: The rest of the family
sections.intro: Optional values answer “is there a value?”. Close relatives answer “and if not, why?”. All of them chain the same way; the Monads page explains how.

items.name: Result, Either
items.text: Holds a value or an error: `Ok`/`Err` in Rust, `Right`/`Left` in Haskell. Haskell’s docs call `Maybe` a simple error monad where every error is `Nothing`, and say a richer one can be built with `Either`. Chaining stops at the first error and carries it out.

items.name: Validation
items.text: Cats’ `Validated` (Scala) looks like `Either` but collects every error instead of stopping at the first, which suits a form with five bad fields. The price: it isn’t a monad but an applicative functor, so it has no `flatMap`. For a check that needs an earlier result, Cats offers `andThen`, which behaves like `Either`’s `flatMap`.

items.name: Try
items.text: Scala’s `Try[T]` is a computation that may have failed by throwing. It is either `Success(value)` or `Failure(exception)`, which turns exception-throwing code into a value you can pass around and chain.

items.name: Nullable value types
items.text: Some languages also mark plain numbers as optional: C# has had nullable value types (`int?`) since C# 2.0 in 2005, long before nullable reference types arrived in C# 8.

sections.title: Where `Optional` belongs in Java
body: Java’s API documentation is explicit: `Optional` “is primarily intended for use as a method return type where there is a clear need to represent ‘no result,’ and where using null is likely to cause errors”, and a variable of type `Optional` should never itself be `null`. Unlike Kotlin’s `?`, nothing in the compiler enforces either rule.

Teams still argue about fields and parameters. Oracle’s Inside Java Newscast described the camps, from never using `Optional` to using it everywhere, and reported that its developers, Brian Goetz and Stuart Marks among them, recommend the middle: only return values, and only where a missing result is error-prone. The case against fields and parameters is practical: `Optional` isn’t serializable, callers must wrap every argument, and a caller can still pass `null` for the `Optional` itself. The newscast suggests trying overloads first, then builders or parameter objects.

story: Tony Hoare added the null reference to ALGOL W in 1965. He was designing the first comprehensive type system for references in an object-oriented language, with the goal that every use of a reference would be checked by the compiler, but, in his words, “I couldn’t resist the temptation to put in a null reference, simply because it was so easy to implement.” At QCon London in 2009 he called it his “billion-dollar mistake”: it had “led to innumerable errors, vulnerabilities, and system crashes”. His abstract noted that newer languages such as Spec# had added declarations for non-null references, “the solution, which I rejected in 1965.”

Functional languages such as Haskell offered the alternative: `Maybe` makes absence an ordinary value that must be matched. Mainstream languages followed in the 2010s. Java 8 (2014) added `Optional` for return types. Kotlin built null safety into its type system, citing the billion-dollar mistake, and reached 1.0 in 2016. Swift made `nil` “the absence of a value of a certain type” rather than a pointer, and Rust left null references out entirely.

Languages with a large existing codebase retrofitted the check instead. TypeScript 2.0 (September 2016) added `strictNullChecks`; its announcement joked that “if null is the billion dollar mistake, undefined only doubles our losses.” C# 8.0 (September 2019) added nullable reference types as warnings from static analysis, leaving run-time behaviour unchanged, so old code still compiles and teams can opt in.

choices.choice: Put absence in the type, not in every reference
choices.why: Hoare’s original goal for ALGOL W was that all use of references should be checked automatically by the compiler. A null that fits every reference type defeats that check; a separate type (`Option`, `String?`) restores it.

choices.choice: A `?` on the type rather than a wrapper object
choices.why: Kotlin, C#, Swift and TypeScript had to interoperate with code and libraries that already use null. Marking the type keeps the same values at run time: TypeScript erases its `!` from the emitted JavaScript, and C#’s analysis is compile-time only.
C# added the feature 17 years after 1.0. Making it static analysis with warnings means existing code keeps compiling and running the same, and a project opts in with `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`.

choices.choice: Java’s `Optional` only as a return type
choices.why: It was added as a library class, not a language feature, so it can’t stop a `null` `Optional`. Its docs scope it to return values where `null` is likely to cause errors.
